questions.question: What are debugging and logging and why do they matter from day one?
questions.title: Debugging & Logging Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Debugging is the process of finding why software behaves incorrectly and verifying a fix. Logging records selected runtime events so behavior can be investigated later or in another environment. Debuggers, tests, logs, metrics, and traces answer different questions; choosing the least intrusive useful signal is part of the work.

sections.title: Two complementary views of a failure
sections.content:
**Debugging** is the investigation used to explain a defect and find its cause. **Logging** records selected events while the program runs, so behavior can be examined later when an interactive debugger was not attached.

They support different moments. A debugger can pause a reproducible local failure and inspect live state. Logs can show that request `req-42` entered an endpoint, called a payment adapter, and failed with a timeout in production. Metrics and traces add other views, so logs are an important signal rather than the whole observability system.

A useful workflow starts from evidence: reproduce when possible, follow the error or correlation ID, form one hypothesis, test it, and protect the fix with a regression test. Logging should record enough context for that investigation without exposing secrets or flooding normal traffic.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) the debugging cycle — reproduce the bug reliably, form a hypothesis about the cause, inspect state (debugger, print), test the hypothesis, fix, and verify (including a regression test); (2) the scientific mindset — change one thing at a time and observe, never two; (3) the debugger — a tool to pause execution, inspect variables, and step through code (IDE debugger, jdb); (4) logging levels — TRACE/DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR, each with a purpose, configurable at runtime so you can turn DEBUG on in production without redeploying; (5) structured logging — fields (JSON), not free text, so logs are searchable; (6) log what matters (entry/exit, decisions, errors with context), not every line; (7) the stack trace — the most important clue when something fails.

sections.title: A methodical debug and a leveled, structured log
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: A debugger gives detailed live state but pausing threads can change timing and is rarely suitable for a busy shared system. Logs preserve selected evidence without an interactive session, but excessive volume costs money and can hide the useful signal. Start with a reproducible case and existing evidence, then add targeted instrumentation or attach a debugger only when it answers a specific hypothesis.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Debugging is a methodical hypothesis-test cycle (reproduce → hypothesize → inspect → fix → verify), not random changes.
Change one thing at a time and observe — changing two things confounds the cause.
The debugger (IDE/jdb) pauses execution and inspects state; stepping with a breakpoint beats print-and-rerun.
Logging is leveled (TRACE/DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR), each with a purpose, configurable at runtime without redeploying.
Structured logging (fields, not free text) makes logs searchable; log what matters (decisions, errors with context), not every line.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Debugging is finding and fixing defects, and logging is recording what your program did, and together they're how you understand code that isn't doing what you expect — debugging answers why it's wrong right now, and logging answers what it did before or in production. They matter from day one because you spend more time reading and fixing code than writing it. The debugging method I follow is a hypothesis-test cycle: reproduce the bug reliably, form a hypothesis about the cause, inspect the state with a debugger or a print, test the hypothesis, fix, and verify with a regression test. The rule I stress is change one thing at a time — if you change two and it works, you don't know which one mattered. For logging I use levels — TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR — each with a purpose, and the big win is that levels are configurable at runtime, so I can turn DEBUG on in production without redeploying. I log structured fields, not free text, so the logs are searchable, and I always include context with errors and pass the exception object so the full stack trace prints, because the stack trace is the most important clue when something fails. The trade-off I'm honest about is that random trial-and-error feels fast but rarely finds subtle bugs, while the methodical cycle feels slower but actually works.

questions.question: Why is logging important in a Java backend application?
questions.title: Why Logging Matters in Java Backend
questions.direct_answer: Backend code often runs where a developer cannot inspect it interactively. Logs preserve selected events, errors, and correlation identifiers so a team can investigate what happened across instances and time. They are one observability signal alongside metrics and traces, not the only source of production evidence.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Backends run **headless** — logs are the only window into production behavior.
- Logs enable **debugging, audit trails, monitoring/alerting, and request tracing**.
- Always include **business context** (order/user/request IDs) and stack traces on failures.
- Logs are how you **reproduce the unreproducible** bug.
- Use a real logging framework, not println, so logs are filterable and routable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Logging is essential in a backend because, unlike a program running on your laptop, a backend runs headless on a server — usually across multiple instances — and you can't just watch it or attach a debugger in production. Logs are your eyes into the running system. They're the record of what happened, in what order, and why. I'd point to four concrete uses. First, debugging. Production bugs are often impossible to reproduce locally because they depend on real data or timing, and the logs are what let you reconstruct what actually happened — the real inputs, the sequence of calls, the actual stack trace. Second, audit trails. Logs give you a record of who did what and when, which is important for support and for compliance. Third, monitoring and alerting. Your logs feed dashboards and alerts, so you can see error rates spiking or latency climbing and react before customers complain. Fourth, request tracing. In a system with multiple services, you attach a correlation ID to each request and log it everywhere, so you can follow one user's request end to end across all the services it touched. The thing that separates good logging from bad is context. A line that just says error occurred is useless. A line that says payment failed for order 42, customer 7, with the stack trace attached, is something you can actually debug from months later. So logging isn't optional print statements — it's the core way you understand a system you can't see directly.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A backend may run across containers or machines long after the request that exposed a problem. A useful log keeps evidence such as the event name, result, safe business identifier, correlation ID, and an unexpected exception.

For example, order `842` may fail only on one instance after a payment timeout. Centralized logs can connect the incoming request to the adapter failure without reproducing it immediately. Metrics can show that failures increased, and traces can show latency across services; logs explain selected events in detail.

Logs must be planned. Secret values, raw tokens, passwords, and unnecessary personal data create risk, while excessive low-value events hide the signal and increase cost.

sections.title: What Logging Gives You
sections.content:
blue|Debugging|~Reproduce the unreproducible|see the real inputs|the exact sequence|the actual stack trace
emerald|Audit trail|~Who did what, when|order placed by user 7|payment processed|compliance evidence
amber|Monitoring|~Health + alerts|error rate spikes|latency trends|feed dashboards
violet|Tracing|~Follow one request|correlation ID|across services|end-to-end view

sections.title: A Log Line That Actually Helps Later
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No context**: logging 'error occurred' with no order ID, user ID, or stack trace — useless during an incident.
- **Logging only success**: recording happy paths but not failures, so you're blind exactly when it matters.
- **Using println**: which has no levels, timestamps, or routing, so it can't serve as a real audit trail.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: More detail can shorten an investigation, but it also adds storage cost, processing work, and privacy risk. Keep stable operational events at suitable levels, make temporary diagnostics easy to enable for a narrow scope, and use retention and access controls. Logs complement metrics and traces; they should not be the only record of application health.

questions.question: Why should you use a logging framework instead of System.out.println in Java?
questions.title: Logging Framework vs System.out.println in Java
questions.direct_answer: `System.out.println` writes an unclassified text line to standard output. A logging API creates an event with a level, logger name, parameters, exception data, and provider-supplied metadata and routing. Containers often capture stdout, but a logging framework still supplies filtering and structure without editing each call.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Framework gives **levels, timestamps, context, configuration, routing**; println gives none.
- **Disable in prod with config**, not by deleting code.
- **Parameterized `{}`** avoids building strings for suppressed messages.
- **stdout can vanish** in containers; appenders route to durable sinks.
- **SLF4J + Logback** is the Spring Boot default and just as easy to write.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: You should use a logging framework instead of System.out.println because println is missing everything a production system needs. The biggest gap is log levels. With a framework I tag each message as debug, info, warn, or error, and then I can filter — show only info and above in production, but turn on debug when I'm troubleshooting. println has no concept of that; everything is just text. A framework also adds timestamps automatically, which you need to reconstruct the order of events during an incident, and it adds the logger name so you know which class produced the message. Then there's configuration. With a logger I can change behavior through a config file — turn debug off in production with a single line — whereas with println the only way to stop the output is to find and delete every statement and redeploy. For example, `log.info("Order {} created", orderId)` records the order without building the message when that level is disabled, and the logging configuration can add the time, class, and request ID. A framework can also route output: to a file, as JSON, or to a centralized logging system, while println only goes to standard output, which in a Docker container might not be captured anywhere you can read. There's even a performance angle: frameworks use parameterized messages with curly-brace placeholders, so if debug is turned off, the framework never builds the string — whereas println concatenation always runs. And under heavy load, println is synchronous and can become a surprising bottleneck. The fix is SLF4J with Logback, which is already the default in Spring Boot. It's the same amount of typing as println, but you get levels, timestamps, context, configuration, and routing for free, so there's really no reason to reach for println in real code.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
`System.out.println` can help during a tiny local experiment, and container platforms often capture standard output. Its limitation is the event model: the call has no logging level, logger name, structured fields, or provider-controlled filtering.

With SLF4J, `log.info("Order {} accepted", orderId)` creates a parameterized event. The runtime provider decides whether that level is enabled and how to format or route it. Configuration can raise one package to DEBUG without changing source code.

Applications can still configure the provider to write to stdout, which is common in containers. The difference is not simply the destination; it is the metadata, filtering, formatting, and control around the event.

sections.title: The Gap at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|println|~stdout only|no levels|no timestamps|edit code to disable
emerald|SLF4J + Logback|~configurable|levels + filtering|timestamps + context|files, JSON, remote
blue|Bonus|~performance|{} placeholders|skip work when off|async appenders

sections.title: Without — println Everywhere
With — SLF4J
When println Is Fine
sections.content: Only for throwaway local experiments, tutorials, or a CLI tool whose whole purpose is printing to the console. Anything that runs in CI, staging, or production should use a logger — and using one from the start saves a find-and-replace later.

questions.question: What should you log in a Java backend application?
questions.title: What to Log in a Java Backend Application
questions.direct_answer: Log events needed to operate and investigate the service: lifecycle changes, important business outcomes, dependency failures, rejected requests, and safe correlation identifiers. Record unexpected exceptions once at a meaningful handling boundary. Do not log passwords, session secrets, access tokens, full payment data, or unneeded personal information.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Log **business events, boundary in/out, errors with stack traces, state changes**.
- Always attach **identifiers** (order/user/request ID) for correlation.
- **Never log secrets or PII** — redact before logging.
- Put routine internal detail at **DEBUG**, not INFO.
- Ask: *would I need this line during a 3 AM incident?*

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: My rule for what to log is simple: log what you'd want to have at 3 AM during an incident. Concretely, that's a few categories. First, significant business events — an order was placed, a payment was processed, a user registered. These give you the narrative of what the system is doing. Second, the inputs and outputs at boundaries — when a request comes in and when you call a downstream service — so you can see what data crossed the line. Third, errors, always with the full stack trace and business context. And fourth, important state transitions, like an order moving from pending to shipped. The critical thing is that every one of these should carry identifiers — an order ID, a user ID, a request ID — so that when you're investigating you can correlate all the lines for one transaction. A log line with no identifiers is almost useless. Now the don'ts. Never log secrets or personal data — passwords, authentication tokens, card numbers, or full request bodies that might contain them. That's both a security risk and a compliance violation, so you redact those fields before logging. And don't log every internal detail at INFO; routine stuff like loop iterations or cache hits belongs at DEBUG so it stays out of production logs. The balance I'm aiming for is enough that I can reconstruct any incident, but not so much that the signal gets buried in noise. If I ask myself, would I actually need this line to diagnose a production problem, and the answer is no, it's probably noise or it belongs at DEBUG.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A good log answers what operation occurred, whether it succeeded, and which safe identifier connects it to related work. Examples include `order_created`, a retry after a dependency timeout, or a message moved to a dead-letter queue.

At service boundaries, record safe metadata rather than entire request and response bodies. An order ID, status, duration, and correlation ID are usually more useful and less risky than a serialized customer object. Validate local privacy and audit requirements before treating any user identifier as safe.

Log an unexpected exception with its stack trace at the layer that handles or reports it. Logging the same exception at every layer creates duplicates. Expected validation failures may need a concise event or metric rather than an ERROR stack trace.

sections.title: Log / Don't Log
sections.content:
emerald|Always log|~At INFO|business events|errors + stack traces|with order/user IDs
blue|Log at DEBUG|~Dev detail|method inputs|downstream payloads|state transitions
rose|Never log|~Security risk|passwords + tokens|card numbers|PII / full bodies
amber|Add context|~Correlation|request ID via MDC|timestamps|service name

sections.title: Logging the Right Things with Context
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No identifiers**: 'order failed' with no order or user ID — impossible to investigate.
- **Logging secrets**: card numbers, passwords, tokens, or whole request bodies — a security and compliance breach.
- **Everything at INFO**: dumping internal loop detail at INFO, drowning the real business events.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: An event is useful only if it helps operate, audit, or investigate the service. Too little context makes it impossible to connect related work; too much context raises cost and may expose personal or secret data. Prefer stable event names, safe identifiers, and summaries. Record payload fields only when their operational value and handling rules are clear.

questions.question: What is structured logging and why is it preferred over plain text logs?
questions.title: Structured Logging in Java
questions.direct_answer: Structured logging records named fields such as `event`, `orderId`, and `durationMs` alongside a log event. A provider may encode them as JSON, logfmt, or another machine-readable form. Search and alert tools can query the fields directly instead of parsing changing sentence text, while a human-readable message can still be included.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Structured logging = **key-value/JSON** entries, not freeform sentences.
- Lets log tools **filter, aggregate, and alert by field** without regex.
- Pairs with **MDC** to add `requestId`, `userId` to every line automatically.
- Use `logstash-logback-encoder` or similar to emit JSON in Spring Boot.
- Plain text is fine locally; structured is the norm for shipped production logs.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Structured logging means writing each log entry as machine-readable key-value pairs, usually JSON, instead of a freeform sentence. So instead of logging the sentence user 7 placed order 42 for ninety-nine dollars, I log a JSON object with fields: event is order_placed, userId is 7, orderId is 42, total is 99.99. The reason this is preferred is querying. In production, logs get shipped to a central system like the ELK stack, Splunk, or Datadog, and you want to ask questions like show me all orders over fifty dollars, or all requests that returned a 500. With plain text you'd have to write fragile regular expressions to pull those values out of the sentence, and that breaks the moment someone changes the wording. With structured logging, total and status are real fields, so it's just a simple field query, and you can build dashboards and alerts directly on those fields. Structured logging also pairs really well with MDC, the mapped diagnostic context, which lets you automatically attach things like a request ID and user ID to every log line for a request, so all the entries for one transaction share those fields and you can group them instantly. In a Spring Boot app you'd typically add something like the logstash-logback-encoder to output JSON. For a tiny local script, plain text is fine and more readable, but for any real service whose logs you actually query and alert on, structured logging is the standard because it turns your logs into queryable data instead of just text.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Structured logging** stores named fields with an event instead of hiding every value inside one sentence. A provider may encode those fields as JSON, logfmt, or another format understood by the collection system.

For example, an event can contain `event=order_placed`, `orderId=42`, `status=accepted`, and `durationMs=18`. A search can filter by `status` or aggregate `durationMs` without parsing a changing sentence.

The field names form a small data contract. Keep them consistent, use proper number and boolean types, and avoid serializing whole domain objects. Structure improves queries only when sensitive data is excluded and the schema stays understandable.

sections.title: Plain vs Structured
sections.content:
rose|Plain text|~Human-friendly|freeform sentence|regex to parse|hard to query
emerald|Structured (JSON)|~Machine-friendly|key-value fields|query by field|aggregate + alert
blue|Best of both|~MDC + JSON|requestId field|searchable|dashboards

sections.title: Plain Text — Hard to Query
Structured — Query by Field
When to Use Structured Logging
sections.content: Use structured logging whenever logs are shipped to a **central system** you query and alert on — basically any real production service. It's overkill for a tiny local script. The big win is operational: you can build dashboards, alerts, and ad-hoc queries on fields (`status=500`, `total>1000`) instead of brittle text matching.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Structured fields make queries and dashboards more reliable, but they need a stable schema. Unbounded values can create high-cardinality indexes, duplicate field names break searches, and large payloads increase cost and privacy risk. Keep a small set of well-defined fields, place free text in the message, and version important event contracts when necessary.

questions.question: What is centralized log aggregation and why do teams use it?
questions.title: Centralized Log Aggregation for Java Applications
questions.direct_answer: Centralized log aggregation collects selected log events from application instances into a shared search and retention system. It lets a team investigate one request across instances, create dashboards or alerts, and keep evidence after an instance disappears. Collection is not automatic proof of completeness: buffering, back pressure, outages, retention, access control, and sensitive-data handling still need design.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Modern apps run on **many ephemeral instances** — local files don't scale.
- Pipeline: **emit (JSON) → ship (Filebeat/Fluentd) → store/index (Elasticsearch/Loki/Splunk) → search/alert (Kibana/Grafana/Datadog)**.
- One place to **search, dashboard, and alert** across all instances.
- **Correlation IDs** let you trace a request across services.
- The app just emits **structured logs**; the platform does aggregation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Centralized log aggregation means shipping the logs from every service and every instance into one central, searchable system instead of leaving them as files on individual servers. Teams use it because of how modern applications run. A real backend isn't one process on one machine — it's many instances or containers, often behind a load balancer, and containers are ephemeral, so when one is replaced its local log file just disappears. If a customer reports an issue, you have no idea which of the ten instances handled their request, and you can't SSH into all of them and grep through files. That doesn't scale. So the pattern is a pipeline. Each application emits structured logs, ideally JSON, to standard out or a file. Then a shipping agent — something like Filebeat, Fluentd, or a vendor agent — collects those logs and forwards them. They go into a central store that indexes them, like Elasticsearch, Loki, or Splunk. And on top of that you have a UI like Kibana, Grafana, or Datadog where you can search across every instance at once, build dashboards, and configure alerts. The classic example everyone names is the ELK stack — Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana. The real payoff combines with correlation IDs: because every log line carries a request ID through the MDC, you can search that one ID and instantly see every log line for that request, across all the services it touched. So instead of debugging blind across a fleet of servers, you have one searchable, queryable view of your entire system's behavior.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Centralized log aggregation collects events from application instances into a searchable service. Container stdout collectors, agents, or platform integrations forward events, and the backend indexes or stores them for search, dashboards, and alerts.

This matters when a request can land on any replica. A correlation ID lets an engineer find related events without connecting to each machine. Aggregation also preserves logs after an instance is replaced.

Centralization introduces responsibilities: access control, encryption, retention, cost limits, and redaction. Logs can support request investigation, while distributed tracing is usually a better model for the complete cross-service path and timing.

sections.title: Log Aggregation Pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A1[App instance 1
JSON logs] --> S[Log shipper
Filebeat/Fluentd] A2[App instance 2
JSON logs] --> S A3[App instance 3
JSON logs] --> S S --> St[(Store + index
Elasticsearch/Loki)] St --> UI[Search + dashboards
Kibana/Grafana] UI --> O[On-call: search,
alert, trace by requestId] ```

sections.title: How the Pipeline Works
sections.content:
**1. Emit** — each app writes structured (JSON) logs to stdout or a file.
**2. Ship** — an agent like Filebeat, Fluentd, or the Datadog agent collects and forwards them.
**3. Store & index** — Elasticsearch, Loki, or Splunk indexes the fields so they're fast to query.
**4. Search & alert** — Kibana/Grafana/Datadog give one UI to search across all instances, build dashboards, and fire alerts.

Because every line carries a correlation ID (via MDC), you can follow one request across all the services it touched, in one query.

sections.title: Emitting Logs the Aggregator Can Use
Important trade-off
sections.content: A central system improves cross-instance search and retention but introduces network, storage, indexing, and access-control costs. Forwarders need buffering and back-pressure behavior, and the service needs a plan for collector outages. Limit sensitive fields, control who can search them, choose retention deliberately, and monitor dropped or delayed events.

questions.question: What is MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) in Java logging?
questions.title: MDC in Java Logging
questions.direct_answer: MDC is a provider-supported diagnostic context exposed by SLF4J as key-value data associated with the current thread. A logging pattern or structured encoder must include those keys before they appear in output. MDC does not automatically cross executor, async, or reactive boundaries; copy or bridge context deliberately, and restore or clear values on pooled threads.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **MDC**: key-value diagnostic context used by supported logging providers
- **Output configuration**: the pattern or structured encoder must include MDC fields
- **Thread boundary**: classic MDC does not automatically propagate to executors or reactive work
- **Pooled threads**: restore or clear values so one request cannot leak into the next
- **Scope helper**: `MDC.putCloseable` can remove a temporary key with try-with-resources

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: MDC stands for Mapped Diagnostic Context, and it's a per-thread key-value map that SLF4J and Logback provide. The idea is that you put a value into it once — typically at the very start of a request — and from then on it's automatically attached to every log line produced on that thread, without you having to pass it into each log call. The classic use case is a correlation ID. At the start of an HTTP request, in a servlet filter, I generate a request ID and call MDC.put with the key requestId. Then, anywhere downstream — in the controller, the service, the repository — every log line automatically includes that request ID, because I've configured my log pattern to print the MDC value using the percent-X-curly-brace-requestId syntax. That means when a user reports a problem, I can grab their request ID and instantly pull up every single log line for just that one request, even though it touched a dozen classes. The most important gotcha, and the thing interviewers love to check, is that you must clear the MDC when the request finishes. Application servers use thread pools, so the same thread gets reused for the next request. If you don't call MDC.clear in a finally block, the old request ID leaks into the next request's logs, and now your correlation is wrong and misleading. The other thing to know is that MDC is thread-local, so it doesn't automatically follow you if you spawn a new thread or run something asynchronously — you have to copy the context over yourself. But for normal request-scoped logging, MDC is the clean, standard way to tie all of a request's logs together.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**MDC**—Mapped Diagnostic Context—lets code attach fields such as `requestId` to logging events without passing that value to every log call. The SLF4J API exposes the context, while the active logging provider stores and renders it.

The output configuration must include the MDC field, for example `%X{requestId}`, or use a structured encoder that reads MDC. Setting a value alone does not guarantee that every appender prints it.

Classic MDC is associated with the current thread. Executor tasks, `@Async`, `CompletableFuture`, and reactive pipelines may run elsewhere, so context needs an explicit propagation mechanism suited to that framework. When code places a value on a reusable thread, restore the old context or clear it in `finally`; `MDC.putCloseable` can help scope a value.

sections.title: MDC at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Per-thread map|~Thread-local|key-value pairs|set once|auto-attached
emerald|Use case|~Correlation|requestId|userId|trace one request
amber|Pattern|~%X{key}|in log layout|or JSON field|every line gets it
rose|Gotcha|~Must clear|MDC.clear()|thread pools reuse threads|stale values leak

sections.title: Setting and Clearing MDC in a Filter
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not clearing MDC**: thread pools reuse threads, so a leftover `requestId` leaks into the next request's logs. Always `MDC.clear()` in a `finally`.
- **Expecting it to cross threads**: MDC is thread-local; spawning a new thread or async task loses it unless you copy it over.
- **Putting huge objects in MDC**: keep it to small identifiers, not whole payloads.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: MDC avoids passing a request ID into every logging call, but traditional implementations associate data with a thread. Thread pools can leak stale values unless they are restored or cleared, and asynchronous or reactive work may require explicit context propagation. Keep the context small and confirm that the configured output format actually includes it.

questions.question: What information should every log message include?
questions.title: What Every Log Message Should Include
questions.direct_answer: There is no useful field that every application log call must repeat. The logging system normally adds timestamp, level, and logger; the code should add a stable event or clear message plus only the safe context needed to understand it. Add correlation and business identifiers when relevant, and include an exception stack trace for an unexpected failure at its handling boundary—not for every error-level event.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Provider metadata**: timestamp, level, and logger are normally added by the logging system
- **Application context**: stable event/message plus safe identifiers relevant to that event
- **Correlation**: add a request or trace identifier when work spans several events
- **Exception**: preserve one unexpected stack trace at a meaningful handling boundary
- **Data safety**: exclude secrets and unneeded personal or payment data

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A useful log event needs a clear name or message and the context required to understand that event. The logging system normally adds the timestamp, level, and logger, so application code does not need to repeat them in the sentence. For a payment timeout I might add `orderId`, `requestId`, `dependency=payments`, and the outcome. A startup event needs different fields, so there is no sensible universal list for every call. I attach the exception object when an unexpected failure is handled so the full cause chain is preserved, but I avoid logging the same stack trace at each layer. Secrets, access tokens, passwords, full card data, and unnecessary personal data never belong in the event.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
The logging provider normally supplies transport metadata such as timestamp, level, logger, and sometimes thread. Application code should supply a clear event name or message and the few fields that explain that event.

For an order failure, useful fields might be `orderId`, `requestId`, `dependency=payments`, and `outcome=timeout`. A scheduled startup event may need none of those. Repeating every possible field on every line increases noise and may expose personal data.

Attach the exception object when an unexpected failure is first handled or reported so its type, message, causes, and frames are preserved. Do not log the same stack trace at every layer, and do not use an ERROR stack trace for ordinary validation results.

sections.title: Six Ingredients
sections.content:
blue|Auto by framework|~You don't write these|timestamp|level + class|thread name
emerald|You provide|~The valuable part|clear message|order/user/request IDs|outcome/state
rose|On errors|~Pass the exception|full stack trace|not e.getMessage()|root cause visible
amber|For correlation|~Via MDC|requestId on every line|group a request|across classes

sections.title: A Complete, Useful Log Line
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No identifiers**: 'save failed' with no order/user ID — can't tie it to anything.
- **Losing the stack trace**: logging `e.getMessage()` as a string instead of passing the exception object.
- **Vague messages**: 'something went wrong' tells the on-call engineer nothing actionable.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Repeating every possible field makes events noisy and expensive, while omitting relevant context makes them hard to connect. Let the logging system add timestamp, level, logger, and service metadata. Application code should add a stable event or clear message and only the safe identifiers needed for that event. Avoid unbounded labels, secrets, and duplicated exception logging.
